clue.text: American actor’s spoken line of Shakespeare?

indicators.note: spoken words are heard, so the answer is how the phrase sounds

blocks.note: a line is a row, and Shakespeare is the Bard, so a line of such poets

explanation.surface: An American star delivers a speech from a Shakespeare play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Line of Shakespeare' wants to be a verse; it is a row of Shakespeares. Jason Robards was an Oscar-winning American actor.
explanation.definitionFit: Jason Robards won Oscars for All the President's Men and Julia, a celebrated American film and stage actor.

clue.text: Don’t permit anything short to be worn

indicators.note: something short is cut off before its end, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: to ban is to forbid
all, meaning anything whatever, without its last letter

explanation.surface: A dress code forbids any skimpy clothing being worn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short to be worn' suggests a hemline; 'worn' means hackneyed.
explanation.definitionFit: A banal remark is trite and overused, and worn describes an expression so familiar it has lost its force.

clue.text: Depression has so far not entirely regressed

indicators.note: not entirely means only part of the phrase, so the letters lie within it
to regress is to go backwards, so the letters are read from right to left

blocks.note: the letters running across the word breaks

explanation.surface: A patient's depression has, up to now, partly slipped back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depression' reads as low mood; it is a hollow, as in anatomy.
explanation.definitionFit: In anatomy a fossa is a shallow pit or hollow in a bone, so it is a physical depression.

clue.text: Was once successful in sales — making money no longer

blocks.note: with the opening word, was successful in sales means the past tense of sell
once is one time, and one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A former top salesperson is no longer earning anything.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the opening as 'sold once': the past tense of sell, then the numeral one.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldi is the plural of soldo, an old Italian copper coin long out of circulation, so it is former currency.

clue.text: Niche firm in East London’s cut by 50 per cent

indicators.note: a Cockney from the East End drops the H sound at the start of a word
in means placed within, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: to halve something is to reduce it by half
CO is the abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: A specialist company in London's East End has had its workforce halved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Niche firm' reads as a specialist business, but 'Niche' is the definition. A Cockney is a working-class East Londoner who drops H.
explanation.definitionFit: An alcove is a recess set back into a wall, the same architectural feature as a niche.

clue.text: To get nowhere is to be sufficient with pop groups

blocks.note: if there is enough food it will go round everyone
in means popular, fashionable
circles are social groups or sets

explanation.surface: A cynic says making enough money from music bands is a dead end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop groups' reads as bands; split it into a word for fashionable and a word for sets.
explanation.definitionFit: Going round in circles is an idiom for making no progress, endlessly repeating without arriving anywhere.

clue.text: All there is to follow vermouth, flipping fruit tea!

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the letters run the other way
to follow is to come next in line, so this part is placed at the end

blocks.note: it is short for Italian vermouth, as in gin and it
someone all there is of sound mind

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims that a fruit infusion is all that's left to drink after the vermouth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All there' looks like 'everything'; it means mentally sound. 'Gin and it' is an old British cocktail order.
explanation.definitionFit: A tisane is an infusion of herbs, flowers or fruit made like tea but without tea leaves.

clue.text: For trial, took up with Left: set to agitate

indicators.note: to agitate is to shake or stir, so the letters are tossed into a new order

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for with
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A political activist was taken up for trial alongside left-wingers ready to stir trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Took up' suggests arrest; it means flew an aircraft aloft.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilot who test-flew a new plane took it up into the air to trial its performance.

clue.text: Cheat also, it’s said, getting prison sentence

indicators.note: something said is heard rather than read, so it is the sound that counts

blocks.note: too means also
doing time is serving a prison sentence

explanation.surface: A fraudster also gets locked up, according to reports.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheat' suggests fraud and prison; here it means being unfaithful.
explanation.definitionFit: To two-time a partner is to be unfaithful by secretly seeing someone else, a way of cheating on them.
